questions.questionText: According to Henry's Law, the concentration of a gas dissolved in seawater is:

options.text: Inversely proportional to its partial pressure above the sea
Proportional to its partial pressure above the sea, via an equilibrium constant
Independent of temperature and salinity
Only dependent on the gas's molecular weight

questions.questionText: Why is oxygen more soluble in seawater than nitrogen, despite oxygen having a higher molecular weight (32) than... wait, actually similar to argon (40)?

options.text: Oxygen is monoatomic, making it easier to dissolve
Oxygen is diatomic, so its electron cloud is more easily perturbed by water, increasing solubility
Oxygen reacts chemically with water molecules
Oxygen has a lower molecular weight than nitrogen

questions.questionText: What effect does increasing water temperature have on gas solubility?

options.text: Solubility increases because molecules move closer together
Solubility decreases because higher kinetic energy increases the probability of gas escaping the liquid phase
Solubility remains constant regardless of temperature
Solubility increases uniformly for all gases at the same rate

questions.questionText: What is the role of the ocean 'microlayer' in gas exchange between the atmosphere and the ocean?

options.text: It has no effect on gas exchange, since gases pass freely between phases
It is a thick layer where turbulent mixing dominates gas transfer
It is a thin laminar surface layer that controls the transfer of gases by molecular diffusion, and its thickness decreases at higher wind speeds
It only matters for chemically reactive gases like ammonium and sulphates

questions.questionText: In feature extraction, which level of image analysis focuses specifically on the outline of an object?

options.text: Boundary analysis
Region analysis
Whole image analysis
Texture analysis

questions.explanation: Boundary (shape/external) analysis focuses on the outline of the object, using methods like chain codes, Fourier descriptors, and signatures.

questions.questionText: Which method represents an object's boundary as a wave-like signal for shape description?

options.text: Euler number
Fourier Descriptors
PCA
Global Histogram statistics

questions.explanation: Fourier Descriptors represent the boundary as a wave, making them a boundary-level feature extraction method used for tasks like digit recognition and silhouette matching.

questions.questionText: Which feature extraction level would be most appropriate for distinguishing a rough fabric surface from a smooth one?

options.text: Boundary analysis
Region analysis
Whole image analysis
Chain code analysis

questions.explanation: Region (texture/internal) analysis focuses on the content inside the object boundary and includes texture analysis methods, used to distinguish smooth surfaces from rough ones like fabric.

questions.questionText: The Euler number, used in region-based feature extraction, specifically measures what property of an object?

options.text: The object's center of mass
The object's orientation angle
The number of holes in the object
The perimeter length of the object

questions.explanation: The Euler number is a region-based moment method that measures the number of holes in an object.

questions.questionText: PCA (Principal Component Analysis), used for whole image analysis such as Eigenfaces, differs from region and boundary methods primarily because it:

options.text: Requires segmentation of the object's boundary first
Only analyzes texture inside the object
Analyzes the image as a single entity without segmentation
Represents the boundary as a chain of directional moves

questions.explanation: Whole image analysis, including PCA for eigen-images, analyzes the image as a single entity without segmentation, unlike boundary or region methods which require identifying object outlines or interiors.

questions.questionText: Otsu's method determines the optimal global threshold by:

options.text: Minimizing the mean intensity of the whole image
Maximizing the variance between the foreground and background pixel classes
Averaging the highest and lowest pixel intensities
Minimizing the number of edge pixels detected

questions.explanation: Otsu's method is an algorithm that automatically finds the optimal global threshold T by maximizing the variance between the two classes of pixels (foreground and background).

questions.questionText: What is a key advantage of Otsu's method compared to manual thresholding techniques?

options.text: It adapts locally to varying illumination across the image
It works equally well on unimodal and multimodal histograms
It automatically selects the threshold without requiring user interaction
It is unaffected by noise in the image

questions.explanation: One of the pros of Otsu's method is that it is automatic, requiring no user interaction or manual tuning.

questions.questionText: Otsu's method works best when the image histogram is:

options.text: Unimodal, with a single sharp peak
Bimodal, with two distinct peaks
Multimodal, with several evenly spaced peaks
Flat, with uniformly distributed intensities

questions.explanation: A key limitation of Otsu's method is the bimodal requirement: it only works well if the image histogram has two distinct peaks, and fails on unimodal or multimodal histograms.

questions.questionText: Why might Otsu's method produce a poor threshold when the object of interest is very small compared to the background?

options.text: The algorithm cannot process images with more than one object
Small objects increase the computational cost beyond feasible limits
The corresponding histogram peak may be swamped, leading to a poor threshold
The method requires objects to occupy at least half of the image

questions.explanation: Under the size imbalance con, if the object is very small compared to the background (or vice versa), the histogram peaks may be swamped, leading to a poor threshold.

questions.questionText: Like all global thresholding methods, Otsu's method fails under which condition?

options.text: When the image contains only grayscale values
When lighting varies across the image, such as with shadows
When the image resolution is too high
When the foreground and background have identical colors

questions.explanation: The content notes that, like all global thresholding methods, Otsu's method fails if the lighting varies across the image, such as with shadows (uneven illumination).

questions.questionText: What is the primary effect of a log transformation on an image's pixel values?

options.text: It expands dark pixel values while compressing higher-level values
It compresses dark pixel values while expanding higher-level values
It equally expands both dark and bright pixel values
It inverts all pixel values in the image

questions.explanation: The log transformation (s = c · log(1 + r)) is used to expand the values of dark pixels in an image while compressing the higher-level values.

questions.questionText: Why is the log transformation essential for visualizing Fourier Spectra?

options.text: Because Fourier Spectra only contain dark pixel values
Because without it, the wide value range makes the spectrum appear as a single white dot
Because Fourier Spectra require gamma correction instead
Because the log transformation removes noise from the frequency domain

questions.explanation: Fourier Spectra values range from 0 to millions, and without a log transformation the spectrum looks like a single white dot; with log, the details become visible.

questions.questionText: What makes the gamma (power-law) transformation more versatile than the log transformation?

options.text: It can only be applied to medical images
The shape of its curve can be tuned via the gamma value
It always compresses dark pixel values
It does not require a constant c in its formula

questions.explanation: The gamma transformation is described as more versatile than log because the curve shape can be tuned, unlike the fixed shape of the log transformation.

questions.questionText: In gamma correction, when would a gamma value less than 1 (y < 1) be used?

options.text: To darken washed-out images by expanding bright values
To brighten shadows by expanding dark values, such as in medical X-rays or underexposed photos
To visualize Fourier Spectra more effectively
To equally balance dark and bright pixel values

questions.explanation: When gamma is less than 1, the transformation brightens shadows by expanding dark values, which is used for medical X-rays or underexposed photos.

questions.questionText: For which type of filter kernel is spatial domain filtering typically faster than frequency domain filtering?

options.text: Large filter kernels
Small filter kernels, such as 3x3 or 5x5
Filters designed to remove periodic noise
Filters requiring global periodic noise removal

questions.explanation: Spatial domain filtering is much faster for small filter kernels (e.g., 3x3 or 5x5), while frequency domain filtering becomes advantageous for large filters.

questions.questionText: Why does frequency domain filtering become extremely fast for large filters?

options.text: Because it avoids using the Fourier Transform entirely
Because of the Convolution Theorem, filtering becomes simple multiplication
Because it does not require an inverse transform
Because large filters do not require padding

questions.explanation: Based on the Convolution Theorem, filtering in the frequency domain is just simple multiplication, making it extremely fast for large filters.

questions.questionText: What type of noise removal is possible in the frequency domain but impossible in the spatial domain?

options.text: Random Gaussian noise
Global periodic noise, like moiré patterns
Salt-and-pepper noise
Edge-related noise artifacts

questions.explanation: The frequency domain allows easy removal of global periodic noise, like moiré patterns, which is impossible in the spatial domain.

questions.questionText: What artifact can appear in frequency domain filtering when ideal filters are used?

options.text: Wrap-around errors from insufficient convolution
Ringing, also known as the Gibbs phenomenon
Excessive blurring of edges
Loss of color information

questions.explanation: Frequency domain filtering can introduce artifacts like ringing (Gibbs phenomenon) if ideal filters are used.

questions.questionText: Why is padding required when performing filtering in the frequency domain?

options.text: To avoid wrap-around errors
To reduce the computational overhead of the FFT
To eliminate the need for an inverse FFT
To make complex global filtering easier to design

questions.explanation: A listed con of frequency domain filtering is that padding is required to avoid wrap-around errors.

questions.questionText: Morphological operators are primarily used for which type of image processing task?

options.text: Pre- or post-processing of binary images (masks)
Converting color images to grayscale
Compressing images for storage
Enhancing frequency domain representations

questions.explanation: Morphological operators are used primarily for pre- or post-processing binary images (masks), such as cleaning noise, separating objects, and filling holes.

questions.questionText: Which morphological operator is used to separate objects that are accidentally touching?

options.text: Dilation
Closing
Erosion
Opening's dilation step

questions.explanation: Erosion shrinks or thins objects by removing pixels from boundaries, which is used in practice to remove small noise and separate touching objects.

questions.questionText: What is the practical effect of the Dilation operator on a binary image?

options.text: It shrinks objects and removes isolated noise pixels
It grows objects, filling small holes and bridging gaps between broken lines
It extracts the skeleton of an object without changing its size
It separates touching objects into distinct regions

questions.explanation: Dilation grows or thickens objects by adding pixels to boundaries, and its practical use is filling small holes and bridging gaps between broken lines.

questions.questionText: The Opening operator, defined as Erosion followed by Dilation, is practically used to:

options.text: Fill internal holes without expanding the object's outer size
Remove small noise objects without changing the size of the main object
Bridge gaps between broken lines in an image
Thicken all objects uniformly across the image

questions.explanation: Opening (Erosion followed by Dilation) is practically used to remove small noise objects without changing the size of the main object.

questions.questionText: How does the Closing operator (Dilation followed by Erosion) differ from Opening in its practical effect?

options.text: Closing removes small noise objects, while Opening fills internal holes
Closing fills internal holes and gaps without expanding the object's outer size, while Opening removes small noise without changing the main object's size
Closing and Opening both perform the exact same operation in a different order with identical results
Closing shrinks objects permanently, while Opening only affects boundary pixels temporarily

questions.explanation: Closing (Dilation followed by Erosion) fills internal holes and gaps without expanding the object's outer size, whereas Opening (Erosion followed by Dilation) removes small noise objects without changing the size of the main object.

questions.questionText: Compared to second-order derivative operators, first-order gradient operators (like Sobel and Prewitt) are:

options.text: More sensitive to noise
Less sensitive to noise
Equally sensitive to noise
Unable to detect edges in noisy images

questions.explanation: First-order gradient operators are less sensitive to noise than second-order operators, which is listed as one of their key advantages.

questions.questionText: What information can first-order gradient operators calculate easily that makes them useful for edge detection?

options.text: Only the direction of the edge, not its strength
Both the magnitude and direction of the edge
The exact single-pixel location via zero-crossing
The rotational invariance of the image

questions.explanation: First-order gradient operators calculate both magnitude (strength) and direction (angle) of the edge easily.

questions.questionText: A major drawback of first-order derivative operators for edge detection is that they:

options.text: Produce thick edges that require post-processing to pinpoint the exact boundary
Cannot calculate edge direction
Generate double edges at ramp transitions
Are extremely sensitive to noise

questions.explanation: A con of first-order operators is that they produce 'thick' edges (multiple pixels wide) that require post-processing (thinning) to pinpoint the exact boundary.

questions.questionText: The Laplacian (2nd order derivative) operator can achieve single-pixel edge precision through which mechanism?

options.text: Gradient magnitude thresholding
Zero-crossing detection
Directional angle averaging
Post-processing thinning

questions.explanation: The Laplacian can produce thinner edges with single pixel precision via zero-crossing, unlike first-order operators which produce thicker edges.

questions.questionText: What is a key disadvantage of using the Laplacian (2nd order derivative) for edge detection?

options.text: It cannot detect edge direction or magnitude at all
It is rotationally variant (anisotropic)
It is extremely sensitive to noise and can generate double edges at ramp transitions
It always produces thicker edges than first-order operators

questions.explanation: The Laplacian's cons include being extremely sensitive to noise and generating 'double edges' at ramp transitions.
